p: Good evening, my dear friend, and welcome to the Brackets and Braces primer. This is a series of ten short lectures, and I have been looking forward to it more than almost anything else in the course. A great many people go through school without anybody explaining plainly what brackets are for. They see round ones, square ones and curly ones, and feel they have wandered into a hedge. By the end of these ten lectures, brackets will feel like old friends. That is a promise, and Euclid is my witness, though he is asleep.
## Grouping in ordinary speech

We group words all the time without noticing. Imagine a waiter in a Strand chop-house asking: would you like tea, or coffee with milk? Does that mean tea, or else coffee-with-milk? Or tea-or-coffee, and either way with milk? In speech, we sort it out with pauses and tone of voice. Tea, pause, or coffee with milk. Or: tea or coffee, pause, with milk.
Written mathematics cannot pause or change its tone. So it uses brackets instead. Brackets are written pauses. They say: this part belongs together.
## Parcels in brown paper

Here is a picture to keep for the whole primer, and indeed for the whole course. Imagine a brown-paper parcel tied with string, the sort the post office delivers. Inside are several small things. When you carry the parcel, you carry it as one object. Brackets are the brown paper. Whatever is inside a pair of brackets is wrapped up and treated as one single thing.
## Brackets come in pairs

A bracket has two halves: an opening bracket at the start of the group and a closing bracket at the end. On paper, a round opening bracket curves like the left side of a circle, and the closing bracket curves the other way. Together they hug whatever is between them.

When I read a formula aloud, I tell you where each bracket opens and closes with a tone, so that I never need to clutter the formula with the word bracket. If you prefer words, you may choose them in the settings. Here is our first example.
The brackets wrap up two plus three into a parcel. The parcel is worth five. Then five is multiplied by four, giving twenty.
## Meet the tones
Let us hear the tones on their own. Here is the opening round bracket. Notice that it rises.
⟦\tone{round-open}⟧
And the closing round bracket. Notice that it falls.
⟦\tone{round-close}⟧
Rising to open, falling to close, like a door swinging open and then shut, or like a question and its answer. Here they are together, as though wrapping something invisible.
⟦\tone{round-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{round-close}⟧
?? While I pour the tea. If you hear a rising tone, then some words, then a falling tone, what has happened?
=> A bracket has opened, some things have been grouped inside it, and the bracket has closed. Everything between the two tones is one parcel.
## Why bother?

You might ask why we need brackets at all. Could we not simply work from left to right? The trouble is that without brackets, the same string of numbers can mean different things, just like the waiter's question. Listen to these two.

The first is five times four, which is twenty. The second is two plus twelve, which is fourteen. The same numbers and the same signs, but different parcels, give different answers. Brackets are how mathematics says exactly what it means.
?? Work this one in your head: open bracket, ten minus four, close bracket, times two.
=> The parcel is ten minus four, which is six. Then six times two is twelve.
## A little history

Brackets are younger than you might think. Brackets of various shapes appear in Italian books of the sixteenth century, but for a long time mathematicians preferred to draw a bar over the top of the grouped terms, called a vinculum, which is Latin for a bond or a chain. It was only in the eighteenth century, with Leibniz and especially Euler, that brackets became the common habit. Euler, as you will discover, made a great many things in mathematics into the common habit. The vinculum survives in one place you know well: the long roof of the square root sign, which groups everything underneath it.
## The golden rule
Here is the golden rule of brackets, which you will hear again and again. Work out what is inside the brackets first. Treat the inside as one thing. Then carry on with the rest.
?? One more. Three times, open bracket, one plus four, close bracket.
=> The parcel is one plus four, which is five. Three times five is fifteen.
## Summary

Brackets group things, like brown-paper parcels, so they are treated as one. They come in pairs, opening and closing, and in this app the opening tone rises and the closing tone falls. The golden rule: inside first. Next time, we meet the question of what to do when there are no brackets at all: the order of operations, known in British schools as BIDMAS or BODMAS, and best explained, I find, by a visit to a royal kitchen. Until then, my dear friend, good night.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight, a story. When there are no brackets in a calculation, how do we know what to do first? Mathematicians agree on an order, a sort of etiquette, and in British schools it is remembered by the word BIDMAS, or sometimes BODMAS. I find it easiest to explain by way of a royal kitchen.
## The royal kitchen
Imagine the kitchen of a great palace on the evening of a state banquet. The kitchen has a strict order of precedence, as rigid as any at court.
First of all come the sealed hampers, sent down from the royal apartments. Nothing else may be touched until every hamper has been opened and dealt with. These are the Brackets.
Next comes the head chef, who deals in powers: doubling and trebling recipes, squaring the trays. These are the Indices, which is another word for powers.
Then come the two senior cooks, of exactly equal rank, Division and Multiplication. Neither outranks the other. They work along the bench from left to right, whoever comes first.
Last come the two kitchen maids, also of equal rank, Addition and Subtraction. They too work along the bench from left to right.

So: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction. B, I, D, M, A, S. BIDMAS. Some schools say O for Orders instead of I for Indices, hence BODMAS. In America they say PEMDAS, with P for Parentheses. Same kitchen, different livery.
## Hearing it in action
⟦2+3\times 4⟧

No brackets, no powers. Multiplication outranks addition, so three times four first, twelve, then two plus twelve, fourteen. Not twenty. If you wanted twenty, you would need a hamper: brackets around two plus three.
?? While I pour. Ten minus two times three.
=> Multiplication first: two times three is six. Ten minus six is four.
## Powers before multiplying

The head chef goes before the cooks: two squared is four, then three times four is twelve. Not six squared, which would be thirty-six. If you wanted thirty-six, you would need brackets around three times two.
## Equal rank, left to right
Here is where many people trip. Division and multiplication have equal rank. They are done in order from left to right.
⟦12\div 3\times 2⟧

Left to right: twelve divided by three is four, then four times two is eight. Not twelve divided by six, which would be two. The D before M in BIDMAS does not mean division comes first. It is only that the letters must go in some order. Likewise, addition and subtraction are done left to right.
Ten minus three is seven, plus two is nine. Not ten minus five.
?? Twenty divided by four times five.
=> Left to right: twenty divided by four is five, then five times five is twenty-five.
## A longer example
First the hamper: seven minus three is four. Then the head chef: four squared is sixteen. Then the cooks: two times sixteen is thirty-two. Then the maids: five plus thirty-two is thirty-seven.
?? Your turn. Three plus, open bracket, two plus four, close bracket, times five.
=> Hamper first: two plus four is six. Then six times five is thirty. Then three plus thirty is thirty-three.
## Why have rules at all?

These rules are a convention, an agreement, like driving on the left in England. Nobody discovered that multiplication comes before addition; mathematicians agreed it, because it makes the most common expressions shortest to write. In algebra we write things like three x plus two, meaning three times x, then add two. The convention lets us leave out brackets that would otherwise be everywhere.

The tidy acronyms themselves are quite modern; I never heard BIDMAS in my schooldays, though the conventions themselves were settled long before. My schoolmaster simply said "powers, then times and divide, then add and take away", and rapped the desk at each one.
## When in doubt, use brackets

Here is a piece of practical wisdom. When you write mathematics, and there is any doubt, add brackets. Brackets are never wrong, merely sometimes unnecessary. A good writer of mathematics, like a good writer of English, prefers to be clear rather than terse.
## Summary

The order of operations is Brackets, Indices, then Division and Multiplication together from left to right, then Addition and Subtraction together from left to right. Brackets override everything. Next time, we watch round brackets at work, doing their many different jobs. Until then, my dear friend, mind your precedence.

Good evening, my dear friend. Round brackets are the everyday workhorses of mathematics, the hansom cabs of notation, always about, carrying all sorts of passengers. In Britain they are simply called brackets; in America, parentheses. Tonight we follow them through a day's work. They have five jobs.
## Job one: do this first
We know this job already. Brackets say: do this part first.
Brackets first: eight plus four is twelve. Then twelve divided by three is four.
?? While I pour. Without the brackets, eight plus four divided by three means something different. What?
=> Division would go first: four divided by three is one and a third. Plus eight is nine and a third. Quite different from four.
## Job two: hidden multiplication
When a number sits right next to a bracket, with no sign between, it means multiply. Mathematicians are lazy writers and leave out the times sign whenever they can.
In plain words: three lots of the parcel. The parcel is five, so the answer is fifteen. Two brackets side by side also mean multiply.
Three times four: twelve.
In algebra this job is everywhere. Three, bracket, x plus one, means three times the whole of x plus one. In the sixth part of this primer we shall see how to unwrap such a parcel.
?? Two, open bracket, six minus one, close bracket.
=> The parcel is five. Two times five is ten.
## Job three: protecting a negative number
Brackets can wrap up a negative number so that its minus sign stays attached. Listen carefully to these two; they sound similar and are quite different.

In the first, the whole of minus three is in the parcel, and the whole parcel is squared: minus three times minus three is plus nine. In the second, there is no parcel. The powers come before everything else, so only the three is squared, making nine, and then the minus sign is applied: minus nine. This catches out a great many people, and a good many calculating machines too, I am told.
?? Open bracket, minus two, close bracket, cubed.
=> Minus two times minus two times minus two. The first two make plus four; times minus two makes minus eight.
## Job four: f of x
Here is a job where brackets do not mean multiply at all. In the lectures on functions, we shall meet expressions like this.

This is read "f of x". The f is the name of a rule, a function, and the brackets hold what the rule is applied to. It is not f times x. Think of f as a machine and the brackets as its hopper. Put x into the f machine. When I read these aloud, I shall say "f of" before the bracket, so you can tell.

How do you know whether brackets mean multiply or "of"? From the letter outside. Letters like f, g and h are, by long custom, names of functions. Euler, in the eighteenth century, was the one who made f of x the standard way of writing it.
## Job five: coordinates
Round brackets also hold pairs of numbers that mark a position, called coordinates. A point three steps across and four steps up is written like this.
The comma separates the across number from the up number. Here the brackets are simply a container, holding a pair together like two eggs in a box.
?? A point is written, open bracket, five, two, close bracket. How far across is it, and how far up?
=> Five across and two up. The first number is across, the second is up.
## Telling the jobs apart

Five jobs, then: do this first; hidden multiplication; keeping a negative number together; f of x; and coordinates. You can tell which job a bracket is doing from what surrounds it. A number in front: multiply. A function name in front: "of". A comma inside: coordinates. A lonely minus sign inside: a protected negative. And always, whatever the job, the parcel is treated as one thing.
## A word on Euclid the cat
Euclid has taken to sitting in a cardboard box by the stove. I explained to him that he is a parcel, treated as one thing. He agreed entirely. He considers himself one thing, and a superior one.
## Summary

Round brackets mean do this first. A number next to a bracket means multiply. Brackets keep a negative number together, so minus three, bracketed, squared, is plus nine. Function brackets, as in f of x, mean "apply to", not multiply. And brackets hold coordinates. Next time, we meet square brackets and curly braces, and brackets inside brackets, with tones that climb as the parcels nest. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight, parcels within parcels. You know the Russian dolls that open to reveal a smaller doll, and inside that another? Or the Chinese puzzle boxes that were so fashionable in London drawing rooms when I was young? Mathematics does the same with brackets, and tonight we learn to open them in the right order.
## Brackets inside brackets

There are two parcels here, one inside the other. You heard the inner bracket's tone a little higher than the outer one: that is how you know it is a parcel inside a parcel. The rule: open the innermost parcel first. Four minus one is three. Now the outer parcel: three plus three is six. Then two times six is twelve.
?? While I pour. Ten minus, open bracket, two times, open bracket, one plus two, close, close.
=> Innermost first: one plus two is three. Then two times three is six. Then ten minus six is four.
## Different shapes for clarity

When brackets are nested, a page full of round brackets becomes hard to read: you lose track of which closing bracket belongs to which opening one. So printers have long used different shapes for different levels. Round brackets innermost, then square brackets, then curly braces outermost. Square brackets have square corners; curly braces look like a pair of wavy moustaches.
Here a round bracket sits inside a square one. In plain words: three times the square parcel, and inside the square parcel, two times x plus one, then take away four.
With the tones, each shape has its own voice. Round brackets, you will remember, are a soft low note. Square brackets are a brighter middle note.
⟦\tone{square-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{square-close}⟧
And curly braces ring like a high chime.
⟦\tone{curly-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{curly-close}⟧
## Three levels

Three levels: a curly parcel, containing a square parcel, containing a round one. Listen to the tones climb as we go deeper and descend as we come out, like walking up a staircase and down again. Innermost first: three plus two is five. Then one plus five is six. Then two times six is twelve. Then twelve take five is seven.
In the settings, you can choose to have deeper brackets move to the left and right instead of climbing in pitch, which some listeners find clearer with headphones. Try both in the Sound gallery.
?? Try a three-level one slowly. Curly brace, five times, square bracket, two plus, round bracket, three minus one, close round, close square, close curly.
=> Innermost: three minus one is two. Then two plus two is four. Then five times four is twenty.
## Counting the balance

Brackets must balance. Every opening bracket must have a closing partner, and they close in the reverse order to the way they opened. The last one opened is the first one closed, like a stack of plates: you take the top plate off first.

Here is a trick blind mathematicians and careful proof-readers both use. Count as you go. Add one for each opening bracket and take one away for each closing bracket. The count tells you how deep you are. If it ever goes below zero, something has closed that never opened. If it does not end at zero, something was never closed. With the tones, you can hear this count: the pitch rises with each opening and falls with each closing, and the formula should end where it began.
?? Count this one: open, open, close, open, close, close. Does it balance?
=> The count goes one, two, one, two, one, zero. It ends at zero and never goes below, so it balances.
## A historical note

The habit of using different shapes for different levels grew up with printing. A printer setting type by hand needed clarity, and so did a reader by candlelight. Different shapes make it much easier for the eye, and in our case for the ear, to match each closing bracket with its partner.
## Euclid and the boxes

Euclid the cat, I regret to say, has discovered the principle of nesting. There is a hat box inside a tea chest in the box room, and he sits in the hat box, inside the tea chest, looking out with the expression of a cat who has reached the innermost level and intends to stay there.
## Summary

When brackets nest, work from the innermost outwards. Different shapes, round inside square inside curly, make nesting clearer; in this app each has its own tone, and deeper brackets climb in pitch. Brackets must balance, and closing happens in reverse order. Count up for each opening and down for each closing. Next time, curly braces in their other great role: holding sets. Good night, my dear friend.
Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight curly braces step out of the background and take a starring role. Their most famous job is holding sets.
## What is a set?

A set is simply a collection of things, gathered together and treated as one. The things in a set are called its elements or members. The days of the week form a set. So do the primes less than ten. We write a set by listing its elements inside curly braces.
You heard the bell-like tone of the curly brace opening and closing. In plain words: the set containing two, three, five and seven.

Two rules about sets. The order does not matter: two, three, five, seven is the same set as seven, five, three, two. And repeating an element changes nothing: a thing is either in the set or not. A set is like a guest list, not a queue.
?? While I pour. Is the set containing one, two and three the same as the set containing three, one and two?
=> Yes. Order does not matter in a set. They are the same set.
## Belonging
To say that something belongs to a set, mathematicians use a little symbol like a rounded letter E, read "is in" or "is an element of".
In plain words: three is an element of the set one, two, three.
## Big sets and the three dots
Some sets are too big to list. The counting numbers go on forever. We write the first few and then three dots, which I read as "and so on".

There is also a set with nothing in it at all, called the empty set. It is written as a pair of curly braces with nothing inside. Aunt Hester would have disapproved of an empty set, as she disapproved of zero, but it is very useful. The set of cats who dislike fish, for example, is the empty set.
## Set-builder notation
Instead of listing elements, we can describe a set by a rule. This is called set-builder notation.

In plain words: the set of all x such that x is greater than nought. The colon inside the braces is read "such that". So this is the set of all positive numbers. Some books use an upright line instead of a colon, and it means the same.
?? How would you describe, in words, the set of x such that x is between one and five?
=> All the numbers bigger than one and smaller than five. The rule after "such that" tells you who is invited.
## Union and intersection
Two sets can be combined in two important ways. The union of two sets contains everything that is in either set. The intersection contains only what is in both.

The union is written with a sign like a letter U, a cup that holds everything; the intersection with a sign like an upside-down U, a cap. In the first, the union holds one, two, three and four; three is not written twice. In the second, the intersection holds only three, the one element they share.

Imagine two circles drawn overlapping on paper, one for each set. The union is everything inside either circle. The intersection is the lens-shaped overlap in the middle. These pictures are called Venn diagrams, after John Venn of Cambridge, who described them in a paper of 1880. Venn was, I may say, also an enthusiastic builder of machines; he built one for bowling cricket balls, which bowled out a leading Australian batsman when the touring team visited Cambridge in 1909. That last fact sounds invented, but it is told in respectable accounts of his life, and I gather it was reported at the time.
?? The set of people who play the piano is one circle, and the set of people who sing is another. Who is in the intersection?
=> People who both play the piano and sing.
## Sets underneath everything

In the later nineteenth century, Georg Cantor in Germany built a whole theory of sets, and showed that some infinite sets are bigger than others, which caused a great deal of upset. In the twentieth century, mathematicians came to describe almost all of mathematics in the language of sets. So these humble curly braces turn out to hold up the entire building. We shall hear more of Cantor in our lecture on infinity.
## Summary

Curly braces hold sets: collections where order does not matter and repeats are ignored. The symbol "is in" shows membership. Set-builder notation describes a set by a rule, with the colon read "such that". The union holds everything in either set; the intersection holds only what is in both. Next time, the most useful bracket skill in algebra: expanding, which means unwrapping parcels. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we unwrap parcels. In algebra, a number standing outside a bracket multiplies everything inside it, and writing out the result without the bracket is called expanding, or multiplying out. It is one of the most useful skills in all of algebra, and you already know it, for it is the grid method from base camp, in a new coat.
## The number outside multiplies everything inside
In plain words: three lots of the parcel x plus two. Three lots of x, and three lots of two. So three x plus six.

Picture three identical bags, each holding an apple, which we shall call x, and two oranges. Altogether you have three apples and six oranges. Unwrapping the bags does not change what you have; it only lays it out on the table.

The great mistake, which every teacher has seen a thousand times, is to multiply only the first thing inside: three x plus two. That is like unpacking three bags and counting only one bag's oranges. The number outside must greet everyone in the parcel, like a good host at a party.
?? While I pour. Expand five, bracket, x plus four.
=> Five times x is five x, and five times four is twenty. Five x plus twenty.
## Why it works
This is the distributive law, which we met when multiplying twenty-three by four: four lots of twenty, plus four lots of three. Here is the same idea with numbers, to check.
Three times twelve is thirty-six, and three tens plus three twos is thirty-six. The law holds.
## Negatives inside and out
With a minus sign inside, the multiplying still reaches everything.
Four times minus three is minus twelve. And with a minus outside, every sign inside flips, because minus times plus is minus, and minus times minus is plus.
In plain words: minus two times x is minus two x; minus two times minus five is plus ten. This is where the sign rules from our lecture on minus times minus pay their rent.
?? Expand minus three, bracket, x plus two.
=> Minus three x, and minus three times two is minus six. Minus three x minus six.
## A letter outside
The thing outside can be a letter too.
x times x is x squared, and x times five is five x.
## Two brackets: four handshakes
Now the grand case: two brackets multiplied together.

Every term in the first bracket must meet every term in the second. There are two terms in each, so four meetings, which I like to call handshakes. x meets x: x squared. x meets three: three x. Two meets x: two x. Two meets three: six.
Then tidy up: three x and two x are the same kind of thing, so they combine into five x. The answer: x squared plus five x plus six.

This is exactly the grid method from base camp. When we multiplied twenty-four by thirteen, we split them into twenty and four, and ten and three, and made four meetings. Here x plus two and x plus three are split the same way.
?? Expand, bracket, x plus one, bracket, x plus four.
=> Four handshakes: x squared, four x, x, and four. Tidy the middle: x squared plus five x plus four.
## A picture in words

If you like pictures, imagine a rectangle whose width is x plus two and whose height is x plus three. Divide it into four smaller rectangles: an x by x square, an x by three strip, a two by x strip, and a little two by three corner. Their areas are x squared, three x, two x and six. Add them and you have the area of the whole rectangle. The Greeks did algebra in exactly this way, with rectangles, two thousand years before anyone wrote x.
## With negatives
Four handshakes: x times x, x times one, minus four times x, minus four times one. Then x minus four x is minus three x.
?? Expand, bracket, x minus two, bracket, x minus three. Careful with the last handshake.
=> x squared, minus three x, minus two x, and minus two times minus three is plus six. So x squared minus five x plus six.
## Summary

To expand, the number or letter outside multiplies everything inside: no one in the parcel is left out. Watch the signs: a minus outside flips every sign inside. For two brackets, make all four handshakes, then tidy up like terms. It is the grid method, and the Greeks' rectangles, in algebraic dress. Next time, we do it backwards: factorising, which means wrapping things up again. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Last time we unwrapped parcels. Tonight we wrap them up again. Factorising means writing an expression as things multiplied together, in brackets. It is expanding run backwards, like watching a magic lantern show in reverse, and it is how we shall solve many equations in the foothills.
## Taking out a common factor
What do six x and nine have in common? Both can be divided by three. So take the three outside the bracket, and put what remains inside.
In plain words: three lots of two x plus three. Check by expanding: three times two x is six x, three times three is nine. Always check by expanding; it costs a moment and saves a blunder.
The thing we take out should be the highest common factor, the biggest thing every term shares. It might include letters.
Both terms contain an x, so x comes outside.
?? While I pour. Factorise ten x plus fifteen.
=> Both are divisible by five. Five, bracket, two x plus three.
## Two brackets: the reverse handshake

Last time, bracket x plus two, bracket x plus three, expanded to x squared plus five x plus six. Look at the numbers. The six at the end came from two times three. The five in the middle came from two plus three. So to factorise x squared plus five x plus six, we look for two numbers that multiply to six and add to five. Two and three.

Such an expression, with an x squared, is called a quadratic. Factorising quadratics is a little puzzle: find the pair. It is the sort of puzzle the Victorians printed in their periodicals, and Mrs Blewitt does them with her morning tea.
?? Factorise x squared plus seven x plus ten.
=> Two numbers multiplying to ten and adding to seven: two and five. So bracket x plus two, bracket x plus five.
## When signs are negative
If the last number is positive but the middle is negative, both numbers are negative.
Minus two times minus three is plus six, and minus two plus minus three is minus five.
If the last number is negative, the two numbers have opposite signs.
Four times minus three is minus twelve; four plus minus three is plus one.
?? Factorise x squared minus x minus six. Two numbers multiplying to minus six and adding to minus one.
=> Minus three and two. So bracket x minus three, bracket x plus two.
## The difference of two squares
Here is a pattern so pretty it has its own name.

Expand the right-hand side: x squared, minus three x, plus three x, minus nine. The middle terms cancel exactly, leaving x squared minus nine. So whenever you see one square taken from another, it factorises into a plus bracket and a minus bracket. This is called the difference of two squares.

It has a party trick with numbers. Forty-one times thirty-nine? That is, bracket forty plus one, bracket forty minus one, which is forty squared minus one squared, sixteen hundred minus one, which is one thousand five hundred and ninety-nine. Done in a flash.
?? Use the trick. Twenty-one times nineteen.
=> Twenty squared minus one squared. Four hundred minus one, three hundred and ninety-nine.
## Why factorise?

Here is the reason factorising matters so much. Suppose two things multiplied together make nought. Then one of them must be nought: no other numbers multiply to nothing. So if bracket x plus two, bracket x plus three, equals nought, then either x plus two is nought or x plus three is nought, so x is minus two or minus three. Factorising turns one hard equation into two easy ones. We shall use this in the lectures on quadratics.
## Summary

Factorising is expanding backwards. Take out the highest common factor. For a quadratic, find two numbers that multiply to the last number and add to the middle number. The difference of two squares splits into a plus bracket and a minus bracket. Always check by expanding. Next time, a different use of brackets altogether: describing ranges of numbers, where a square bracket means "in" and a round one means "out". Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight brackets take on a new and rather elegant job: describing stretches of the number line. And here, for once, round and square brackets mean quite different things.
## A stretch of road

Remember the number line, the long road with milestones. An interval is a stretch of that road: all the numbers between two milestones. Not only the whole numbers, but every fraction and decimal in between as well, all the infinitely many points.
We write an interval by giving its two ends, separated by a comma, inside brackets. The question is whether the end milestones themselves are included. And the shape of the bracket tells us.
## Square means in, round means out
A square bracket means the end is included. A round bracket means the end is left out.
The interval from two to five, with both ends included: two, five, and everything in between.

The interval from two to five with both ends left out: everything strictly between two and five, but not two or five themselves. Yes, this looks exactly like the coordinates of a point. Mathematicians, alas, reuse their brackets shamelessly, and you must tell from the context which is meant.
Here is a way to remember. A square bracket has corners that grip, like a vice; it holds on to the end. A round bracket curves away, letting the end slip off.
?? While I pour. Is the number five in the interval, square bracket two, comma five, round bracket?
=> No. The round bracket at five lets it slip. Two is in, five is out.
## Mixed intervals
The two ends can have different brackets. This is called half-open.
From nought to one, including nought but not one. Everything from nought up to, but not quite reaching, one. Zero point nine nine nine is in. One is not.

Why would anyone want such a thing? Think of ages. A child is "aged seven" from her seventh birthday up to, but not including, her eighth. On the morning of her eighth birthday, she is no longer seven. So "aged seven" is a half-open interval of time: square at seven, round at eight. Nature is full of half-open intervals; Mrs Blewitt's shop, which is open from nine until, but not including, half past five, as anyone who has arrived at half past five can testify.
## Infinity takes a round bracket
Some intervals go on forever.
⟦[3,\infty)⟧

From three onwards, forever: three and every number bigger. Infinity always takes a round bracket, because infinity is not a milestone you can stand on. You can never reach it, so you can never include it. The square bracket at three says three is included.
All the negative numbers: everything below nought, not including nought.
?? How would you describe, in words, the interval, round bracket five, comma infinity, round bracket?

An interval says the same thing as an inequality, which we shall meet properly in the foothills.

Intervals are the natural language for where a formula makes sense. When we reach functions, we shall say things like: this rule works for every x in the interval from nought to infinity. ## Confusion five: the famous internet quarrel
In your century, so my reading ticket informs me, a puzzle like this one caused enormous and bad-tempered arguments.

One camp says: brackets first, three; then six divided by two is three, times three is nine. Another camp says: the two stuck to the bracket is a single parcel, two times three is six, so six divided by six is one.

Who is right? Under the strict school rule, division and multiplication going left to right, the answer is nine. But many mathematicians and some old textbooks treat a number glued to a bracket as binding more tightly, giving one. The honest answer is that the expression is badly written. No sensible mathematician would write it. They would write it as a fraction, or add brackets, so that there is no doubt.

In mathematics and computer programming, the order of operations is a collection of conventions about which arithmetic operations to perform first in order to evaluate a given mathematical expression.

These conventions are formalized with a ranking of the operations. The rank of an operation is called its precedence, and an operation with a higher precedence is performed before operations with lower precedence. Calculators generally perform operations with the same precedence from left to right, but some programming languages and calculators adopt different conventions.
A formula is omitted here.

For example, multiplication is granted a higher precedence than addition, and it has been this way since the introduction of modern algebraic notation. When exponents were introduced in the 16th and 17th centuries, they were given precedence over both addition and multiplication and placed as a superscript to the right of their base.

These conventions exist to avoid notational ambiguity while allowing notation to remain brief and uncluttered. Where it is desired to override the precedence conventions, or even simply to emphasize them, parentheses can be used. If multiple pairs of parentheses are required in a mathematical expression (such as in the case of nested parentheses), the parentheses may be replaced by other types of brackets to avoid confusion, as in [2 × (3 + 4)] − 5 = 9.

These conventions are meaningful only when the usual notation (called infix notation) is used. When functional or Polish notation is used for all operations, the order of operations results from the notation itself.
## Conventional order

The order of operations, that is, the order in which the operations in an expression are usually performed, results from a convention adopted throughout mathematics, science, technology, and many computer programming languages. It is summarized as:
Parentheses; Exponentiation; Multiplication and division; Addition and subtraction.

This means that to evaluate an expression, one first evaluates any sub-expression inside parentheses, working from inside to outside if there is more than one set. Whether inside parentheses or not, the operation that is higher in the above list should be applied first. Operations of the same precedence are conventionally evaluated from left to right.

If each division is replaced with multiplication by the reciprocal (multiplicative inverse), then the associative and commutative laws of multiplication allow the factors in each term to be multiplied together in any order. Sometimes multiplication and division are given equal precedence, or sometimes multiplication is given higher precedence than division; see § Mixed division and multiplication below. If each subtraction is replaced with the addition of the opposite (additive inverse), then the associative and commutative laws of addition allow terms to be added in any order.

The radical symbol ⟦√⟧, which signifies a square root, is traditionally extended by a bar (the vinculum) over the radicand; this avoids the need for parentheses around the radicand. Other functions use parentheses around the input to avoid ambiguity. The parentheses can be omitted if the input is a single numerical variable or constant, as in the case of ⟦sin x = sin(x)⟧ and ⟦sin π = sin(π)⟧. Traditionally this convention extends to monomials; thus, ⟦sin 3x = sin(3x)⟧ and even a long formula, but ⟦sin x + y = sin(x) + y⟧, because ⟦x + y⟧ is not a monomial. However, this convention is not universally understood, and some authors prefer explicit parentheses. Some calculators and programming languages require parentheses around function inputs, while others do not.
Parentheses and alternate symbols of grouping can be used to override the usual order of operations or to make the intended order explicit. Grouped symbols can be treated as a single expression.

## Mnemonics

Mnemonic acronyms are often taught in primary schools to help students remember the order of operations. The acronym PEMDAS, which stands for Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction, is common in the United States and France. Sometimes the letters are expanded into words of a mnemonic sentence such as "Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally". The United Kingdom and other Commonwealth countries may use BODMAS (or sometimes BOMDAS), standing for Brackets, Of, Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction, with "of" meaning fraction multiplication. Sometimes the O is instead expanded as Order, meaning exponent or root, or replaced by I for Indices in the alternative mnemonic BIDMAS. In Canada and New Zealand BEDMAS is common.

These mnemonics may be misleading when written this way. For example, misinterpreting any of the above rules to mean "addition first, subtraction afterward" would incorrectly evaluate the expression ⟦a − b + c⟧ as ⟦a − ( b + c )⟧, while the correct evaluation is ⟦( a − b ) + c⟧. These values are different when ⟦c ≠ 0⟧.

In Germany, the convention is simply taught as Punktrechnung vor Strichrechnung, "dot operations before line operations" referring to the graphical shapes of the symbols · (multiplication), ∶ (division), + (addition), and − (subtraction). This avoids the potential for the above misunderstanding.

Mnemonic acronyms have been criticized for not developing a conceptual understanding of the order of operations and not addressing students' questions about its purpose or flexibility. Students learning the order of operations via mnemonic acronyms routinely make mistakes, as do some pre-service teachers. Even when students correctly learn the acronym, a disproportionate focus on memorization of trivia crowds out substantive mathematical content. The acronym's procedural application does not match experts' intuitive understanding of mathematical notation: mathematical notation indicates groupings in ways other than parentheses or brackets and a mathematical expression is a tree-like hierarchy rather than a linearly "ordered" structure; furthermore, there is no single order by which mathematical expressions must be simplified or evaluated and no universal canonical simplification for any particular expression, and experts fluently apply valid transformations and substitutions in whatever order is convenient, so learning a rigid procedure can lead students to a misleading and limiting understanding of mathematical notation.
## Calculators

Different calculators follow different orders of operations. Many simple calculators without a stack implement chain input, working in button-press order without any priority given to different operations, give a different result from that given by more sophisticated calculators.

Calculators may associate exponents to the left or to the right. For example, the expression a^b^c is interpreted as a on the TI-92 and the TI-30XS MultiView in "Mathprint mode", whereas it is interpreted as (⟦a^{b}⟧) on the TI-30XII and the TI-30XS MultiView in "Classic mode".

An expression like 1/2x is interpreted as 1/(2x) by TI-82, as well as many modern Casio calculators (configurable on some like the fx-9750GIII), but as (1/2)x by TI-83 and every other TI calculator released since 1996, as well as by all Hewlett-Packard calculators with algebraic notation. While the first interpretation may be expected by some users due to the nature of implied multiplication, the latter is more in line with the rule that multiplication and division are of equal precedence.
When the user is unsure how a calculator will interpret an expression, parentheses can be used to remove the ambiguity.

Order of operations arose due to the adaptation of infix notation in standard mathematical notation, which can be notationally ambiguous without such conventions, as opposed to postfix notation or prefix notation, which do not need orders of operations. Hence, calculators utilizing reverse Polish notation (RPN) using a stack to enter expressions in the correct order of precedence do not need parentheses or any model-specific order of execution.
## Programming languages

Most programming languages use precedence levels that conform to the order commonly used in mathematics, though others, such as APL and Smalltalk, have no operator precedence rules (in APL, evaluation is strictly right to left; in Smalltalk, it is strictly left to right).
A formula is omitted here.

Furthermore, because many operators are not associative, the order within any single level is usually defined by grouping left to right so that 16/4/4 is interpreted as (16/4)/4 = 1 rather than 16/(4/4) = 16; such operators are referred to as "left associative".

Dennis Ritchie, creator of the C language, said of the precedence in C (shared by programming languages that borrow those rules from C, for example, C++, Perl, and PHP) that it would have been preferable to move the bitwise operators above the comparison operators. Many programmers have become accustomed to this order, but more recent popular languages like Python and Ruby do have this order reversed. ## History

The order of operations emerged progressively over centuries. The rule that multiplication has precedence over addition was incorporated into the development of algebraic notation in the 1600s, since the distributive property implies this as a natural hierarchy. As recently as the 1920s, the historian of mathematics Florian Cajori identifies disagreement about whether multiplication should have precedence over division, or whether they should be treated equally. The term "order of operations" and the "PEMDAS/BEDMAS" mnemonics were formalized only in the late 19th or early 20th century, as demand for standardized textbooks grew.

Ambiguity about issues such as whether implicit multiplication takes precedence over explicit multiplication and division in such expressions as a/2b, which could be interpreted as a/(2b) or (a/2) × b, implies that the conventions are not yet completely stable.

In mathematics, the distributive property of binary operations is a generalization of the distributive law, which asserts that the equality
$$ x ⋅ ( y + z ) = x ⋅ y + x ⋅ z
is always true in elementary algebra.
For example, in elementary arithmetic, one has
Therefore, one would say that multiplication distributes over addition.

This basic property of numbers is part of the definition of most algebraic structures that have two operations called addition and multiplication, such as complex numbers, polynomials, matrices, rings, and fields. It is also encountered in Boolean algebra and mathematical logic, where each of the logical and (denoted ⟦∧⟧) and the logical or (denoted ⟦∨⟧) distributes over the other.
## Definition
Given a set ⟦S⟧ and two binary operators ⟦∗⟧ and ⟦+⟧ on ⟦S ,⟧
the operation ⟦∗⟧ is left-distributive over (or with respect to) ⟦+⟧ if, given any elements ⟦x , y , \text{ and } z⟧ of ⟦S ,⟧
the operation ⟦∗⟧ is right-distributive over ⟦+⟧ if, given any elements ⟦x , y , \text{ and } z⟧ of ⟦S ,⟧
and the operation ⟦∗⟧ is distributive over ⟦+⟧ if it is left- and right-distributive.
When ⟦∗⟧ is commutative, the three conditions above are logically equivalent.
## Meaning
The operators used for examples in this section are those of the usual addition ⟦+⟧ and multiplication ⟦⋅ .⟧
If the operation denoted ⟦⋅⟧ is not commutative, there is a distinction between left-distributivity and right-distributivity:
$$ a ⋅ ( b ± c ) = a ⋅ b ± a ⋅ c \text{ (left-distributive) }
$$ ( a ± b ) ⋅ c = a ⋅ c ± b ⋅ c \text{ (right-distributive) }
In either case, the distributive property can be described in words as:
To multiply a sum (or difference) by a factor, each summand (or minuend and subtrahend) is multiplied by this factor and the resulting products are added (or subtracted).

If the operation outside the parentheses (in this case, the multiplication) is commutative, then left-distributivity implies right-distributivity and vice versa, and one talks simply of distributivity.

## Distributivity and rounding

In approximate arithmetic, such as floating-point arithmetic, the distributive property of multiplication (and division) over addition may fail because of the limitations of arithmetic precision. For example, the identity ⟦1 / 3 + 1 / 3 + 1 / 3 = ( 1 + 1 + 1 ) / 3⟧ fails in decimal arithmetic, regardless of the number of significant digits. In mathematics, an interval is the set of all real numbers lying between two fixed lower or upper bounds ("endpoints" or boundary points) with no "gaps". For example, the set of real numbers consisting of ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, and all numbers in between is an interval, denoted ⟦[0, 1]⟧ and called the unit interval. An interval may contain neither endpoint (called an open interval), both endpoints (called a closed interval), or either endpoint (called a semi-open or semi-closed interval).

The intervals just described are the bounded intervals. Often intervals are also allowed to extend without bound in one or both directions, with the unbounded side being denoted by a positive or negative infinity symbol. The set of all positive real numbers is an interval in this sense, denoted ⟦(0, ∞)⟧; the set of all real numbers is an interval that is unbounded on both ends, denoted ⟦(-∞, ∞)⟧.

Intervals are ubiquitous in mathematical analysis. For example, they occur implicitly in the epsilon-delta definition of continuity; the intermediate value theorem asserts that the image of an interval by a continuous function is an interval; integrals of real functions are defined over an interval; and so on For example, interval arithmetic consists of computing with intervals instead of real numbers for providing a guaranteed enclosure of the result of a numerical computation, even in the presence of uncertainties of input data and rounding errors.
Intervals can be defined more generally on any totally ordered set, such as integers or rational numbers. The notation of integer intervals is considered in the special section below.
## Definition of an interval

An interval is a subset of the real numbers that contains all real numbers lying between any two numbers of the subset. Examples are the numbers ⟦x⟧ from one to two, ⟦1 ≤ x ≤ 2⟧, and the numbers ⟦y⟧ greater than 10, that is ⟦y > 10⟧. Under this definition, the empty set and the entire set of real numbers are both intervals.

The endpoints of an interval are its supremum (least upper bound), and its infimum (greatest lower bound), if they exist as real numbers. If the infimum does not exist and the interval is not empty, one says often that the corresponding endpoint is negative infinity, written ⟦− ∞ .⟧ Similarly, if the supremum of a non-empty interval does not exist, one says that the corresponding endpoint is positive infinity, written ⟦+ ∞ .⟧

Non-empty intervals are completely determined by their endpoints and whether each endpoint belongs to the interval. This is a consequence of the least-upper-bound property of the real numbers, which implies that if the elements of a non-empty interval are all less than some finite value, then the interval has a supremum. This characterization is used to specify intervals by means of interval notation, where a square or rounded bracket (parenthesis) indicates whether or not an endpoint belongs to the interval.

## Degenerate intervals

A degenerate interval is any set consisting of a single real number (that is an interval of the form ⟦[a, a]⟧). Some authors include the empty set in this definition. A real interval that is neither empty nor degenerate is said to be proper, and has infinitely many elements.
## Bounded intervals

An interval is said to be left-bounded or right-bounded, if there is some real number that is, respectively, smaller than or larger than all its elements. An interval is said to be bounded, if it is both left- and right-bounded; and is said to be unbounded otherwise. Intervals that are bounded at only one end are said to be half-bounded. The empty set is bounded, and the set of all reals is the only interval that is unbounded at both ends. Bounded intervals are also commonly known as finite intervals.

Bounded intervals are bounded sets, in the sense that their diameter (which is equal to the absolute difference between the endpoints) is finite. The diameter may be called the length, width, measure, range, or size of the interval. The size of unbounded intervals is usually defined as ⟦+∞⟧, and the size of the empty interval may be defined as ⟦0⟧ (or left undefined).
The centre (midpoint) of a bounded interval with endpoints ⟦a⟧ and ⟦b⟧ is ⟦(a + b)/2⟧, and its radius is the half-length ⟦|a - b|/2⟧. These concepts are undefined for empty or unbounded intervals.
## Categorisation by minimum and maximum elements

An interval is said to be left-open if and only if it contains no minimum (an element that is smaller than all other elements); right-open if it contains no maximum; and open if it contains neither. The set of non-negative reals is a closed interval that is right-open but not left-open.

An interval is said to be left-closed if it has a minimum element or is left-unbounded, right-closed if it has a maximum or is right unbounded; it is simply closed if it is both left-closed and right closed.
## Sub-intervals and related constructions
An interval ⟦I⟧ is a subinterval of interval ⟦J⟧ if ⟦I⟧ is a subset of ⟦J⟧. An interval ⟦I⟧ is a proper subinterval of ⟦J⟧ if ⟦I⟧ is a proper subset of ⟦J⟧.

The interior of an interval ⟦I⟧ is the largest open interval that is contained in ⟦I⟧; it is also the set of points in ⟦I⟧ which are not endpoints of ⟦I⟧. The closure of ⟦I⟧ is the smallest closed interval that contains ⟦I⟧; which is also the set ⟦I⟧ augmented with its finite endpoints.
For any set ⟦X⟧ of real numbers, the interval enclosure or interval span of ⟦X⟧ is the unique interval that contains ⟦X⟧, and does not properly contain any other interval that also contains ⟦X⟧.

## Segments and intervals

There is conflicting terminology for the terms segment and interval, which have been employed in the literature in two essentially opposite ways, resulting in ambiguity when these terms are used. ## Properties

The intervals are precisely the connected subsets of ⟦ℝ .⟧ It follows that the image of an interval by any continuous function from ⟦ℝ⟧ to ⟦ℝ⟧ is also an interval. This is one formulation of the intermediate value theorem.
The intervals are also the convex subsets of ⟦ℝ .⟧ The interval enclosure of a subset ⟦X ⊆ ℝ⟧ is also the convex hull of ⟦X .⟧

The closure of an interval is the union of the interval and the set of its finite endpoints, and hence is also an interval. (The latter also follows from the fact that the closure of every connected subset of a topological space is a connected subset.) In other words, we have
⟦\operatorname{cl} ( a , b ) = \operatorname{cl} ( a , b ] = \operatorname{cl} [ a , b ) = \operatorname{cl} [ a , b ] = [ a , b ] ,⟧

## Dyadic intervals

A dyadic interval is a bounded real interval whose endpoints are ⟦\frac{j}{2^{n}}⟧ and ⟦\frac{j + 1}{2^{n}} ,⟧ where ⟦j⟧ and ⟦n⟧ are integers. Depending on the context, either endpoint may or may not be included in the interval.
Dyadic intervals have the following properties:
The length of a dyadic interval is always an integer power of two.
Each dyadic interval is contained in exactly one dyadic interval of twice the length.
Each dyadic interval is spanned by two dyadic intervals of half the length.
If two open dyadic intervals overlap, then one of them is a subset of the other.
The dyadic intervals consequently have a structure that reflects that of an infinite binary tree.

Dyadic intervals are relevant to several areas of numerical analysis, including adaptive mesh refinement, multigrid methods and wavelet analysis. Another way to represent such a structure is p-adic analysis (for ⟦p = 2⟧).
## Real analysis
Intervals are ubiquitous in mathematical analysis, where they are used to express ideas and often occur in key results.

The integral of a real function is defined over an interval. The endpoints of the interval involved usually occur as a subscript and superscript, so the integral ⟦∫_{a}^{b} f ( x ) d x⟧ applies to all ⟦x⟧ belonging to the interval ⟦[ a , b ]⟧.

Intervals occur implicitly in the epsilon-delta definition of continuity of a function ⟦f ( x )⟧: the following account makes them explicit. The function ⟦f⟧ is said to be continuous at a point ⟦a⟧ if for any given value ⟦ε > 0⟧ (epsilon greater than zero) there is a value ⟦δ > 0⟧ (delta greater than zero) for which ⟦f ( x )⟧ lies in the open interval ⟦( f ( a ) − ε , f ( a ) + ε )⟧ whenever ⟦x⟧ is chosen from the interval ⟦( a − δ , a + δ )⟧. The possible values of ⟦ε⟧ and ⟦δ⟧ themselves belong to the unbounded interval ⟦( 0 , + ∞ )⟧, but are usually considered to describe small positive increments. The idea is that a small symmetric interval around point ⟦a⟧ exists where the value of ⟦f ( x )⟧ stays within an open interval of radius ⟦ε⟧ centred around ⟦f ( a )⟧.

The intermediate value theorem captures the intuition that if ⟦f : [ a , b ] → ℝ⟧ is a real valued continuous function on an interval ⟦[ a , b ]⟧ and ⟦d⟧ is any value between ⟦f ( a )⟧ and ⟦f ( b )⟧, then we expect to find a value ⟦c⟧ between ⟦a⟧ and ⟦b⟧ where ⟦f ( c ) = d⟧. For example, if ⟦f ( x ) = x^{2}⟧ is defined on the interval ⟦[ 3 , 4 ]⟧, then given ⟦d = 10⟧ between ⟦f ( 3 ) = 3^{2} = 9⟧ and ⟦f ( 4 ) = 4^{2} = 16⟧, there is a value ⟦c⟧ between ⟦3⟧ and ⟦4⟧ where ⟦f ( c ) = c^{2} = 10⟧.
An equivalent formulation of the theorem asserts that the image of an interval by a continuous function is an interval.

## Confidence intervals

Confidence intervals are important in statistical inference and provide a range of estimated values for an unknown statistical parameter, such as a population mean. Unlike other kinds of interval, a confidence interval is evaluated from a random sample and the interval endpoints are real-valued random variables. A different sample may well give a different result.

When sampling is repeated there is a pre-set probability, known as the confidence level, that a corresponding interval contains the true value of the unknown parameter. For example, if the chosen confidence level were 0.95 and the same sampling procedure were repeated many times, in the long run approximately 95 percent of the resulting intervals would be expected to contain the true value.

The normal distribution provides a simplified illustration. It has a probability density function whose graph is the familiar bell curve. The peak occurs at its mean ⟦μ⟧ (the Greek letter mu) and its width can be described by its standard deviation ⟦σ⟧ (sigma). These two parameters distinguish one bell curve from another, but in all cases the region within two standard deviations either side of the mean represents a probability of approximately 0.95. Every Tychonoff space is embeddable into a product space of the closed unit intervals ⟦[ 0 , 1 ] .⟧ Actually, every Tychonoff space that has a base of cardinality ⟦κ⟧ is embeddable into the product ⟦[ 0 , 1 ]^{κ}⟧ of ⟦κ⟧ copies of the intervals.

## Balls

An open finite interval ⟦( a , b )⟧ is a 1-dimensional open ball with a center at ⟦\frac{1}{2} ( a + b )⟧ and a radius of ⟦\frac{1}{2} ( b − a ) .⟧ The closed finite interval ⟦[ a , b ]⟧ is the corresponding closed ball, and the interval's two endpoints ⟦\{ a , b \}⟧ form a 0-dimensional sphere. Generalized to ⟦n⟧-dimensional Euclidean space, a ball is the set of points whose distance from the center is less than the radius. In the 2-dimensional case, a ball is called a disk.

If a half-space is taken as a kind of degenerate ball (without a well-defined center or radius), a half-space can be taken as analogous to a half-bounded interval, with its boundary plane as the (degenerate) sphere corresponding to the finite endpoint.
## Multi-dimensional intervals

A finite interval is (the interior of) a 1-dimensional hyperrectangle. Generalized to real coordinate space ⟦ℝ^{n} ,⟧ an axis-aligned hyperrectangle (or box) is the Cartesian product of ⟦n⟧ finite intervals. For ⟦n = 2⟧ this is a rectangle; for ⟦n = 3⟧ this is a rectangular cuboid (also called a "box").
Allowing for a mix of open, closed, and infinite endpoints, the Cartesian product of any ⟦n⟧ intervals, ⟦I = I_{1} × I_{2} × ⋯ × I_{n}⟧ is sometimes called an ⟦n⟧-dimensional interval.

A facet of such an interval ⟦I⟧ is the result of replacing any non-degenerate interval factor ⟦I_{k}⟧ by a degenerate interval consisting of a finite endpoint of ⟦I_{k} .⟧ The faces of ⟦I⟧ comprise ⟦I⟧ itself and all faces of its facets. The corners of ⟦I⟧ are the faces that consist of a single point of ⟦ℝ^{n} .⟧
## Convex polytopes

Any finite interval can be constructed as the intersection of half-bounded intervals (with an empty intersection taken to mean the whole real line), and the intersection of any number of half-bounded intervals is a (possibly empty) interval. Generalized to ⟦n⟧-dimensional affine space, an intersection of half-spaces (of arbitrary orientation) is (the interior of) a convex polytope, or in the 2-dimensional case a convex polygon.
## Domains
An open interval is a connected open set of real numbers. Generalized to topological spaces in general, a non-empty connected open set is called a domain.
## Complex intervals
Intervals of complex numbers can be defined as regions of the complex plane, either rectangular or circular.

## Topological algebra

Intervals can be associated with points of the plane, and hence regions of intervals can be associated with regions of the plane. Generally, an interval in mathematics corresponds to an ordered pair ⟦(x, y)⟧ taken from the direct product ⟦ℝ × ℝ⟧ of real numbers with itself, where it is often assumed that ⟦y > x⟧. For purposes of mathematical structure, this restriction is discarded, and "reversed intervals" where ⟦y - x < 0⟧ are allowed. Then, the collection of all intervals ⟦[x, y]⟧ can be identified with the topological ring formed by the direct sum of ⟦ℝ⟧ with itself, where addition and multiplication are defined component-wise.

The identity element of this algebra is the condensed interval ⟦[1, 1]⟧. If interval ⟦[x, y]⟧ is not in one of the ideals, then it has multiplicative inverse ⟦[1/x, 1/y]⟧. Endowed with the usual topology, the algebra of intervals forms a topological ring. The group of units of this ring consists of four quadrants determined by the axes, or ideals in this case. The identity component of this group is quadrant I.
